newsitem.title: SWEDEN: INSTANT VIEW - Economists on Sweden's EMU decision.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW - Economists on Sweden's EMU decision.

text.p: Following are some economists' reactions to Sweden's ruling Social Democrats first official decision on membership of Europe's economic and monetary union (EMU).

Swedish Prime Minister Goran Persson ruled out joining at the start in 1999, as widely expected in the markets, but did not rule out entry in coming years and said Sweden could join between 1998 and 2002.
JAMES MCKAY, PAINEWEBBER
"They have not procluded entry over the next few years so people may regard that as favourable for the market.
It is a touch more favourable than the markets thought after the leaks last week.
But I don't think we will see much of a reaction in the markets today as the markets are starting to close up now."
TOMAS NIEMELA, S-E-BANKEN
"It was what we expected, more or less.
Persson's speech was very cautious and very tame.
I think the view you get is that they will not join before 2003 as there will have to be another election before then. But they are still leaving it open so it could be earlier.
I don't think we will see much movement in the markets from this."
KATHARINE HOYLAND, JP MORGAN

"If what we are told is really all we are seeing right now it implies that as expected we are getting the no in 1999 that we have all been braced for but beyond that the jury is essentially still out.
This is really what I have been expecting. The government would like to retain the flexibility to be able to take the opportunity if the mood swings more into favour than it currently stands.

He has confirmed broadly that he would wait for popular support to back him up before taking the plunge. In what shape or form he would like to see that public support, he has left open all doors and retained all the flexibility. Is it in terms of opinion polls, a general election or even a referendum?
It is positive in that it gives them the flexibility that could be needed if things turn around.
JAN HAGGSTROM, HANDELSBANKEN
"It is pretty much as expected. The government would like to see a shift in public opinion.
However I think it is slightly negative that the referendum was mentioned and even having to do an extra election. I think opening the door for a referendum or for an election is somewhat of a risk.
There are several parties in parliament that want a referendum and that could be very tricky for the government.

The market reaction was close to expectations but also due to the fact that (signs) in Europe over the past couple of weeks have pointed towards a softer EMU. The price of remaining outside the EMU is getting lower day-by-day."
JENS DALSKOV, DEN DANSKE BANK
"I think it was a very cautious statement which was what was expected.
It could be important (that the Prime Minister is talking about a poll) as in Sweden, as in other countries in Europe it would be very nice to ask the population about EMU right now.
Right now the opinioin is slightly against EMU membership but this shows what the risk is to ask the population.

The big attention will be turned towards France and the German situation at the moemnt, I don't think the Swedish decision here will be of much importance in the shortterm. It will only have a slightly longer term effect if anything.
-- Belinda Goldsmith, Stockholm newsroom +46-8-700 1045
